blocks.x: Chapter 5 removed letters from a system one at a time. Chapter 6 opens by putting one in. Prealgebra chapter 7 settled what \(a:b\) says. What is new here is algebraic. Naming the size of one part with a letter turns a ratio statement into an equation, and chapters 4 and 5 already solve equations. Start with a ratio and a total.

A bindery finishes 552 booklets, stapled to sewn in the ratio \(7:5\). Doubling both parts of \(7:5\) gives \(14:10\), which totals \(24\), and tripling gives \(21:15\), which totals \(36\). Keep scaling both parts by the same number until the two counts total \(552\), then enter the number of stapled booklets.
hints: The scaled totals \(24\) and \(36\) are both multiples of \(12\), and \(12\) is \(7+5\). Scaling both parts by the same number multiplies the total by that number as well.
\(552\div 12=46\), so both parts of \(7:5\) get multiplied by \(46\).
blocks.sol: Since \(7+5=12\) and \(552\div 12=46\), both parts get multiplied by \(46\), and the stapled count is \(7(46)=\boxed{322}\). The sewn count is \(5(46)=230\), and \(322+230=552\). Every scaled total is a multiple of \(12\), so dividing \(552\) by \(12\) gives the multiplier in one step instead of testing \(2\), \(3\), \(4\) and on up.

blocks.x: A stadium has 493 seats, covered seats to open seats in the ratio \(9:8\). Write the two counts as \(9k\) and \(8k\) for a single number \(k\), form one equation from the total, and enter the number of covered seats.
hints: Let \(k\) be the size of one part, so the covered seats number \(9k\), the open seats number \(8k\), and the two counts together make \(493\).
\(9k+8k\) collects to \(17k\), so the equation reads \(17k=493\), a one-letter equation of the kind 4.2 solves.
blocks.sol: \(9k+8k=493\) collects to \(17k=493\), so \(k=29\) and the covered seats number \(9(29)=\boxed{261}\). The open seats number \(8(29)=232\), and \(261+232=493\). Naming the part size \(k\) makes the whole problem the single division \(493\div 17\).

blocks.x: The common multiplier. A ratio \(a:b\) says the two amounts are \(ak\) and \(bk\) for one number \(k\), the size of one part. Multiplying both parts by the same number leaves the comparison unchanged, and every pair with that comparison is \(ak\) and \(bk\) for some \(k\), so nothing is lost by writing them that way. With a stated total the counts add to \((a+b)k\), and with three parts to \((a+b+c)k\), so that sum equals the total, one letter and one equation, which chapter 4 finishes in a single division. Scaling by hand finds the same \(k\) one step at a time.

A workshop owns 378 hand tools, all of them hammers or chisels, with hammers to chisels in the ratio \(5:9\). A student computes \(\frac{5}{9}\) of \(378\) and reports \(210\) hammers. Enter the correct number of hammers.
hints: The ratio \(5:9\) compares hammers with chisels, while \(378\) is the total of both kinds. A fraction of that total is taken over both kinds together, not over the chisels alone.
The tools split into \(5+9=14\) equal parts, and the hammers are \(5\) of those parts.
blocks.sol: The tools split into \(5+9=14\) equal parts, so one part is \(378\div 14=27\) tools and the number of hammers is \(5(27)=\boxed{135}\). There are \(9(27)=243\) chisels, and \(135+243=378\). Hammers are \(\frac{5}{14}\) of the tools, not \(\frac{5}{9}\), and with \(210\) hammers only \(168\) chisels remain, more hammers than chisels, the reverse of \(5:9\).

blocks.x: A nursery grows 984 saplings, oak, maple and pine, in the ratio \(6:7:11\). Write the three counts as \(6k\), \(7k\) and \(11k\), and enter the number of pine saplings.
hints: All three counts are built from the same \(k\), so they add to \(6k+7k+11k\), and that sum is \(984\).
blocks.sol: \(6k+7k+11k=984\) collects to \(24k=984\), so \(k=41\) and the pine count is \(11(41)=\boxed{451}\). The others are \(6(41)=246\) oak and \(7(41)=287\) maple, and \(246+287+451=984\). With three parts the sum has one more term than with two, and the rest of the method is the same.

blocks.x: Part to part against part to whole. A ratio \(a:b\) compares the two parts with each other. The first part's share of the whole is \(\frac{a}{a+b}\), since the amounts are \(ak\) and \(bk\), the whole is \((a+b)k\), and cancelling \(k\) from \(\frac{ak}{(a+b)k}\) leaves \(\frac{a}{a+b}\). With three parts it is \(\frac{a}{a+b+c}\). Since \(a+b\) is larger than \(b\), \(\frac{a}{b}\) is larger than \(\frac{a}{a+b}\), so reading a part-to-part ratio as a share of the whole overstates that part. The \(5:9\) hammers are \(\frac{5}{14}\) of the tools and \(\frac{5}{9}\) of the chisels.

blocks.cap: Every block is the same size, and \(k\) is what one block is worth. The ratio \(5:2\) says the first amount is five blocks and the second is two, so the amounts are \(5k\) and \(2k\) and the total is \(7k\), whatever \(k\) turns out to be.

blocks.x: Writing \(x:y=a:b\) is writing \(\frac{x}{y}=\frac{a}{b}\), and that is an equation in two letters. Multiply both sides by \(y\) and then by \(b\), which is 4.4's move done twice, and what is left is \(bx=ay\). Each numerator is multiplied whole, parentheses and all. Neither side is a fraction any more, so \(bx=ay\) is linear in \(x\) and \(y\).

The crates and pallets in a depot are in the ratio \(12:7\), and the depot has 224 pallets. Let \(c\) be the number of crates, so that statement is the equation \(\frac{c}{224}=\frac{12}{7}\). Cross-multiply, solve, and enter the number of crates.
hints: Both sides are single fractions, so clear the denominators. Multiply both sides by \(224\) and then by \(7\), and see what is left.
Clearing gives \(7c=224\times 12\). Since \(224=7\times 32\), divide by \(7\) before multiplying by \(12\), which keeps the numbers small.
blocks.sol: Cross-multiplying \(\frac{c}{224}=\frac{12}{7}\) gives \(7c=2688\), so \(c=\boxed{384}\). Check, \(\frac{384}{224}\) reduces to \(\frac{12}{7}\). In the ratio, crates come first, so \(12\) is the numerator on the same side as \(c\). With the \(12\) and \(7\) swapped the result would be \(\frac{224\times 7}{12}\), not a whole number of crates.

blocks.x: The ratio of \(5(x-4)+3x\) to \(2(x+21)\) is \(3:1\). Collect like terms on each side first, then cross-multiply and enter the value of \(x\).
hints: A ratio of \(3:1\) says the first quantity is \(3\) times the second. Distribute the 2.1 way and combine like terms the 2.4 way on each side, then write that sentence as an equation.
The sides collect to \(8x-20\) and \(2x+42\), so the statement reads \(8x-20=3(2x+42)\).
blocks.sol: Distributing gives \(5x-20+3x=8x-20\) on the left and \(2x+42\) on the right, so \(\frac{8x-20}{2x+42}=\frac{3}{1}\), and cross-multiplying gives \(8x-20=6x+126\), then \(2x=146\) and \(x=\boxed{73}\). Check, \(564\) to \(188\) is \(3\) to \(1\). Writing \(5(x-4)\) as \(5x-4\) instead gives \(x=65\), where the sides are \(500\) and \(172\), not a \(3:1\) pair.

blocks.x: Cross-multiplying a ratio. From \(\frac{x}{y}=\frac{a}{b}\) with \(y\) and \(b\) not zero, multiplying both sides by \(y\) and then by \(b\) gives \(bx=ay\). That is chapter 4's move of multiplying both sides by the same nonzero number, used twice, not a new rule. A numerator with more than one term is multiplied whole, and its parentheses stay. What is left has no fraction and no power, so one such equation in one unknown is chapter 4 work and two in two letters is a chapter 5 system. Every pair \(x=ak\), \(y=bk\) satisfies \(bx=ay\), so the two ways of writing a ratio agree.

An amount can be added to one part, taken from one part, or moved between the two, and the problem states the new ratio. Write the starting amounts as \(ak\) and \(bk\), adjust each by what moved, and that second statement is one equation in \(k\). The two ratios have separate multipliers, so \(13k\) and \(4k\) cannot also be \(10k\) and \(3k\).

A club's juniors and seniors are in the ratio \(11:8\). Then 42 juniors join, no one leaves, and the ratio of juniors to seniors is now \(3:2\). Enter how many juniors the club had before those 42 joined.
hints: The senior count never changes, so write both starting counts from the first ratio and adjust only the junior count.
With \(11k\) juniors and \(8k\) seniors, the counts afterwards are \(11k+42\) and \(8k\), so the second statement is \(\frac{11k+42}{8k}=\frac{3}{2}\).
blocks.sol: With \(11k\) juniors and \(8k\) seniors, the ratio after the 42 join is \(\frac{11k+42}{8k}=\frac{3}{2}\). Cross-multiplying gives \(22k+84=24k\), so \(2k=84\) and \(k=42\), and the juniors before were \(11(42)=\boxed{462}\). Check, the \(336\) seniors are unchanged and \(504:336\) reduces to \(3:2\), so the \(504\) is the count after, not the one asked for. Naming both counts instead gives the system \(8j=11s\) and \(2j+84=3s\), and elimination reaches the same \(j=462\).

blocks.x: Around 350 BCE Eudoxus of Cnidus built the theory of proportion Euclid kept as Book V of the Elements. It compared ratios of lengths where no unit fits a whole number of times into both, such as a square's side and its diagonal.

The same quantity can appear in two ratios with a different number in each. In \(x:y=7:6\) the quantity \(y\) is \(6\) parts, and in \(y:z=9:2\) it is \(9\), and those parts are not the same size. Scale each ratio, both parts by the same factor, until the two numbers for \(y\) agree. The three amounts are then in one ratio \(x:y:z\).
In a stockroom, the ratio of blue crates to green crates is \(15:8\), and the ratio of green crates to red crates is \(8:11\). There are \(165\) blue crates. Enter the number of red crates.
hints: Both ratios use the same number, \(8\), for the green crates, so blue, green, and red fit into one three-part ratio without rescaling either ratio.
Write that three-part ratio, then compare its blue part with the \(165\) actual blue crates to get the multiplier that turns parts into counts.
blocks.sol: Both ratios use \(8\) for green, so blue to green to red is \(15:8:11\). The blue part gives \(15k=165\), so \(k=11\), and the red count is \(11k=\boxed{121}\). Green is \(8k=88\), and the checks pass, \(165:88=15:8\) and \(88:121=8:11\). The chain is direct only because the shared quantity has the same number in both ratios.

blocks.x: For three quantities \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\), \(x:y=16:9\) and \(y:z=6:13\). Enter \(\frac{z}{x}\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: In one statement \(y\) is \(9\) parts and in the other it is \(6\), and those parts are not the same size. Scale each ratio, multiplying both of its parts by the same factor, until the two numbers for \(y\) match.
The least common multiple of \(9\) and \(6\) is \(18\), so double both parts of \(16:9\) and triple both parts of \(6:13\).
blocks.sol: Doubling \(16:9\) gives \(32:18\) and tripling \(6:13\) gives \(18:39\), so with \(y\) at \(18\) parts in both, \(x:y:z=32:18:39\) and \(\frac{z}{x}=\boxed{\frac{39}{32}}\). Stacking the printed numbers gives \(\frac{13}{16}\) instead, which is the trap, since the \(9\) and the \(6\) stand for different sizes of part.

blocks.x: Matching the shared term. Multiplying every part of a ratio by the same nonzero number leaves the comparison unchanged, so \(a:b\) and \(ac:bc\) say the same thing. To combine \(x:y=a:b\) with \(y:z=c:d\), multiply every part of the first by \(c\) and every part of the second by \(b\). In both, \(y\) is then \(bc\) parts, so \(x:y:z=ac:bc:bd\) and \(\frac{z}{x}=\frac{bd}{ac}\), fixed without any amount known. Scaling to any common multiple of \(b\) and \(c\) works, and the least one keeps the numbers small. Scaling only the shared part breaks the statement it came from.

A ratio is one equation in two letters, so neither amount follows from it alone. Adding a second fact about the same two amounts makes a system, and 5.1 counted two equations in two letters as usually enough. It can be a total, a difference, one amount, or the ratio after a change. Cross-multiply the ratio, then use substitution or elimination.

A caterer orders bread rolls and pastries, rolls to pastries in the ratio \(11:6\). Rolls cost 2 dollars each, pastries cost 5 dollars each, and the order comes to 468 dollars. Enter the number of pastries.
hints: The ratio is one fact about the two counts and the total cost is another, so there are two equations in two letters here.

With \(r\) rolls and \(p\) pastries, cross-multiplying the ratio gives \(6r=11p\), and the cost gives \(2r+5p=468\). Tripling the cost equation makes its \(r\)-term \(6r\), which matches the ratio equation.
blocks.sol: Cross-multiplying the ratio gives \(6r=11p\), and the cost gives \(2r+5p=468\). Tripling the cost equation makes it \(6r+15p=1404\), so replacing \(6r\) with \(11p\) leaves \(26p=1404\) and \(p=\boxed{54}\). Then \(r=99\), and \(2(99)+5(54)=468\) checks, though the \(99\) is the roll count and not the ask. Writing the counts as \(11k\) and \(6k\) instead gives \(52k=468\) and the same pair.

blocks.x: A library shelves fiction and nonfiction in the ratio \(11:7\). Then 45 books move from fiction to nonfiction, nothing is added or discarded, and the ratio of fiction to nonfiction reads \(4:3\). Enter how many fiction books the library had before the move.
hints: After the move there are \(45\) fewer fiction books and \(45\) more nonfiction books. Write both starting counts with one letter, using the first ratio.
With \(11k\) fiction and \(7k\) nonfiction, the second ratio gives \(3(11k-45)=4(7k+45)\).
blocks.sol: With \(11k\) fiction and \(7k\) nonfiction the new ratio gives \(\frac{11k-45}{7k+45}=\frac{4}{3}\), so \(33k-135=28k+180\), then \(5k=315\) and \(k=63\). The fiction count before the move was \(11(63)=\boxed{693}\). The nonfiction count was \(441\), and after the move \(648:486\) reduces to \(4:3\). The usual slip is adding the \(45\) to fiction and taking it off nonfiction, which gives \(5k=-315\) and a negative count, so it rules itself out.

blocks.x: Proportion, not size. From \(a:b\) alone every proportion among the amounts is known, the share each part is of the whole and the ratio of any two parts, and not one amount is known. Cross-multiplied the statement is \(bx=ay\), one equation in two letters, which 5.1 already counted as infinitely many pairs, one for each \(k\). So a question about a share of the whole needs only the ratio, while a question about a count always needs a second fact, independent of the first. Restating the same ratio in bigger numbers is not independent and adds nothing.

A festival sells full-price, student, and child tickets. Of the tickets sold, full-price to student is \(7:4\), and student to child is \(6:11\). The festival then sells another 75 child tickets, with no change to the other two counts, and full-price to child is now \(7:9\). Enter the number of student tickets sold.
hints: In one ratio the student tickets are \(4\) parts and in the other they are \(6\), and those parts are not the same size. Combine the two statements into a single three-part ratio before naming any letter.
Matching the student number at \(12\) makes the three-part ratio \(21:12:22\), so the counts are \(21k\), \(12k\) and \(22k\), and the last fact cross-multiplies to \(9(21k)=7(22k+75)\).
blocks.sol: Matching the student number at \(12\) turns \(7:4\) into \(21:12\) and \(6:11\) into \(12:22\), so the counts are \(21k\), \(12k\) and \(22k\). The last fact gives \(\frac{21k}{22k+75}=\frac{7}{9}\), so \(189k=154k+525\), then \(35k=525\) and \(k=15\). The student count is \(12(15)=\boxed{180}\). Check, full-price \(315\) against child \(405\) is \(7:9\). The letter solved for is \(k\), so \(15\) is a part size and not a ticket count.

blocks.x: Every problem here put one letter on the size of a part or cross-multiplied a ratio into \(bx=ay\), and no count came without a second fact. Lesson 6.2, Conversion Factors, uses a ratio of another kind, where the two parts are one amount written in two units. The question there is what such a ratio is worth and what multiplying by it does.

review.x: A crate holds 340 tiles, each one either plain or patterned. The ratio of plain tiles to patterned tiles is \(9:11\). Enter the number of plain tiles.
hints: Read \(9:11\) as \(20\) equal parts of the crate, \(9\) of them plain and \(11\) of them patterned.
Write the counts as \(9k\) and \(11k\). The two counts make up the whole crate, so \(20k=340\).
review.sol: \(9k+11k=340\) gives \(20k=340\), so \(k=17\) and the plain tiles number \(9(17)=\boxed{153}\). The patterned count is \(11(17)=187\), and \(153+187=340\).

review.x: A crate holds pears and quinces and nothing else, in the ratio \(6:11\). Enter the fraction of the fruit that is quinces, in lowest terms.
hints: Nothing pins down the actual counts, so write them as \(6k\) and \(11k\) for some positive number \(k\).
The question asks for quinces out of all the fruit, not quinces out of pears, so the denominator is the total count.
review.sol: The counts are \(6k\) and \(11k\), so the crate holds \(17k\) pieces and the quinces are \(\frac{11k}{17k}\) of it, which is \(\boxed{\frac{11}{17}}\). A common wrong answer is \(\frac{11}{6}\), the quince count over the pear count rather than over the whole crate, and a share of the crate cannot be more than \(1\).

review.x: In a choir, the ratio of altos to sopranos is \(8:13\), and there are 296 altos. Enter the number of sopranos.
hints: Split the choir into equal parts, \(8\) of them altos and \(13\) of them sopranos. Every part is the same size.
The 296 altos fill \(8\) parts, so one part is \(296\div 8=37\) singers.
review.sol: The altos are \(8\) parts, so \(8k=296\) and \(k=37\), which makes the sopranos \(13(37)=\boxed{481}\). Check, \(296:481\) reduces to \(8:13\). No total is stated here and none is needed, since one amount fixes \(k\) on its own.

review.x: A jar holds only amber, jade and onyx marbles, in the ratio \(9:16:5\). Enter the fraction of the marbles in the jar that are jade, in lowest terms.
hints: Nothing pins down the actual counts, so write them as \(9k\), \(16k\) and \(5k\) for one common multiplier \(k\).
The jar holds \(9+16+5\) parts in all, and the jade marbles are \(16\) of them.
review.sol: The counts are \(9k\), \(16k\) and \(5k\), so the jar holds \(30k\) marbles and the jade share is \(\frac{16k}{30k}=\boxed{\frac{8}{15}}\). With three parts the share of the whole is still one part over the sum of all the parts, and \(\frac{16}{9}\) or \(\frac{16}{5}\) would each compare jade with one other colour instead.

review.x: A silo holds 494 sacks of wheat, rye and oats in the ratio \(5:9:12\). Enter the number of sacks of oats.
hints: Write the three counts as \(5k\), \(9k\), and \(12k\) for one common multiplier \(k\). Those three add to \(494\).
Collecting the three terms gives \(26k=494\).
review.sol: Write the counts as \(5k\), \(9k\), and \(12k\). Then \(26k=494\), so \(k=19\) and the oat count is \(12(19)=\boxed{228}\). The other two are \(5(19)=95\) wheat and \(9(19)=171\) rye, and \(95+171+228=494\).

review.x: A workshop stocks screws, bolts and rivets in the ratio \(11:6:4\), and there are 156 bolts. Enter the total number of screws, bolts and rivets.
hints: The bolts are the \(6\) in \(11:6:4\), so \(156\) bolts fill \(6\) equal parts. Divide to find what one part is worth.
One part is \(156\div 6=26\) pieces, and the three counts together are \(11+6+4\) parts.
review.sol: Each part is \(k\) pieces, and the bolts are \(6\) parts, so \(6k=156\) and \(k=26\). The three counts together are \(11+6+4=21\) parts, so the total is \(21\times 26=\boxed{546}\). Counting by kind, that is \(286\) screws, \(156\) bolts and \(104\) rivets, and \(286+156+104=546\).

review.x: The equation \(\frac{x}{84}=\frac{17}{12}\) holds. Cross-multiply and enter \(x\).
hints: Multiplying both sides by \(84\) and then by \(12\) clears both denominators.
review.sol: Cross-multiplying gives \(12x=1428\), so \(x=\boxed{119}\). Cancelling the \(12\) into the \(84\) first turns the whole thing into \(17\times 7\), which is faster than multiplying and then dividing.

review.x: Cross-multiply \(\frac{7x-12}{2x+50}=\frac{5}{3}\), collect the \(x\)-terms on one side and the numbers on the other, and enter \(x\).
hints: The fraction bar groups its whole numerator, so each product needs parentheses around that numerator.
Distributing turns the cross-multiplied equation into \(21x-36=10x+250\), the 4.3 shape with letters on both sides.
review.sol: Cross-multiply, \(3(7x-12)=5(2x+50)\), so \(21x-36=10x+250\), then \(11x=286\) and \(x=\boxed{26}\). Check, at \(x=26\) the fraction is \(\frac{170}{102}\), which reduces to \(\frac{5}{3}\).

review.x: Two accounts hold money in the ratio \(17:8\), and the first holds 288 dollars more than the second. Enter the balance of the smaller account, in dollars.
hints: Write the balances \(17k\) and \(8k\), then say what their difference is in terms of \(k\).
The gap is \(17k-8k=9k\), and that gap is \(288\).
review.sol: With balances \(17k\) and \(8k\), the gap is \(17k-8k=9k\), so \(9k=288\) and \(k=32\), and the smaller balance is \(8(32)=\boxed{256}\). The other balance is \(544\), and \(544-256=288\), with \(544:256\) equal to \(17:8\) in lowest terms. A difference is enough to find \(k\), the same as a total would be.

review.x: A stall sells notebooks and folders in the ratio \(9:7\). Notebooks cost 6 dollars each, folders cost 11 dollars each, and the stall takes 1572 dollars for them. Enter the number of folders sold.
hints: The ratio fixes the two counts up to one multiplier, so write them as \(9k\) notebooks and \(7k\) folders and let the money give the second fact.
The notebooks bring in \(6(9k)\) dollars and the folders \(11(7k)\), and those add to \(1572\).
review.sol: With \(9k\) notebooks and \(7k\) folders, the money gives \(54k+77k=1572\), so \(131k=1572\) and \(k=12\), which makes the folder count \(7(12)=\boxed{84}\). There are \(108\) notebooks, and \(648+924=1572\) checks. The ratio alone fixes neither count, and the takings are the second fact that does.

review.x: Two positive whole numbers are in the ratio \(13:6\), and both are less than \(200\). Enter how many such pairs there are.
hints: Every such pair is \(13k\) and \(6k\) for a positive whole number \(k\), so counting the pairs is the same as counting the allowed values of \(k\).
The larger of the two numbers is \(13k\), so once \(13k\) stays under \(200\) the smaller one does too. Only \(13k\) needs checking.
review.sol: Every such pair is \(13k\) and \(6k\) for a positive whole number \(k\), and \(6k\) is the smaller of the two, so the only condition is that \(13k\) stays under \(200\). Since \(13\times 15=195\) and \(13\times 16=208\), \(k\) can be \(1\) through \(15\), a count of \(\boxed{15}\). Without the limit there would be one such pair for every \(k\), endlessly many.

review.x: In a model kit, pegs and struts come in the ratio \(10:3\), and struts and panels come in the ratio \(3:4\). A batch of these parts has \(76\) panels. Enter the number of pegs in the batch.
hints: Struts appear as \(3\) in both ratios, so the two ratios join with no rescaling.
Combining them gives pegs to struts to panels as \(10:3:4\), and the panels are the \(4\).
review.sol: The struts match at \(3\) in both ratios, so pegs to struts to panels is \(10:3:4\). The panels give \(4k=76\), so \(k=19\) and the pegs number \(10(19)=\boxed{190}\). If the two strut counts had differed, both ratios would need scaling to a common strut count first.

review.x: A field holds 682 plants, all of them corn, beans or squash. Corn to beans is \(6:5\) and beans to squash is \(10:9\). Enter the number of squash plants.
hints: Beans count for \(5\) parts in one ratio and \(10\) parts in the other, so rescale before using the total.
Doubling \(6:5\) gives \(12:10\), so corn to beans to squash is \(12:10:9\).
review.sol: Doubling \(6:5\) gives \(12:10\), which matches the beans in \(10:9\), so corn to beans to squash is \(12:10:9\). The three parts add to \(31\), one part is \(\frac{682}{31}=22\) plants, and squash is \(9(22)=\boxed{198}\). Corn and beans come out to \(264\) and \(220\), and \(264+220+198=682\).

review.x: A survey counts \(m\) walkers, \(n\) cyclists and \(p\) drivers, with \(m\) to \(n\) as \(5:12\) and \(n\) to \(p\) as \(8:9\). Scale so the two numbers for \(n\) agree, then enter \(\frac{p}{m}\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The two numbers standing for \(n\) are \(12\) and \(8\), and the smallest common multiple of \(12\) and \(8\) is \(24\).
Double both parts of \(5:12\) and triple both parts of \(8:9\).
review.sol: Doubling \(5:12\) gives \(10:24\) and tripling \(8:9\) gives \(24:27\), so \(m:n:p=10:24:27\) and \(\frac{p}{m}=\boxed{\frac{27}{10}}\). Using the printed numbers straight gives \(\frac{9}{5}\), which is wrong because \(n\) is \(12\) parts in the first ratio and \(8\) parts in the second.

review.x: A pantry stocks honey jars and jam jars in the ratio \(10:7\). After 48 more honey jars arrive and no new jam jars, the ratio of honey to jam is \(8:5\). Enter the number of jam jars.
hints: The jam count never changes, so call the starting counts \(10k\) honey and \(7k\) jam, then add the 48 to the honey only.
Cross-multiplying \(\frac{10k+48}{7k}=\frac{8}{5}\) gives \(50k+240=56k\).
review.sol: Write the counts as \(10k\) honey jars and \(7k\) jam jars. Then \(\frac{10k+48}{7k}=\frac{8}{5}\), and cross-multiplying gives \(50k+240=56k\), so \(6k=240\), \(k=40\) and the jam count is \(7(40)=\boxed{280}\). Check, the honey counts are \(400\) and \(448\), and \(448:280\) reduces to \(8:5\). The \(400\) is honey, not the count asked for.

review.x: A vault holds silver and copper coins, and the ratio of silver to copper is \(9:4\). The owner removes 32 silver coins and puts in 32 copper coins, after which the ratio of silver to copper is \(5:4\). Enter the number of silver coins the vault held at the start.
hints: Taking out \(32\) silver coins and putting in \(32\) copper coins keeps the total number of coins the same, so only the split between the two changes.
With \(9k\) silver and \(4k\) copper at the start, the new ratio gives \(4(9k-32)=5(4k+32)\).
review.sol: With \(9k\) silver and \(4k\) copper at the start, the new ratio gives \(4(9k-32)=5(4k+32)\), so \(36k-128=20k+160\), then \(16k=288\) and \(k=18\). The starting silver count is \(9(18)=\boxed{162}\). The vault began with \(162\) silver and \(72\) copper, and afterwards \(130:104\) reduces to \(5:4\).

review.x: At a gallery, the ratio of prints to paintings is \(16:7\). Then 26 prints are sold and 13 paintings are added, and the ratio of prints to paintings is now \(5:3\). Enter the total number of prints and paintings after the change.
hints: The ratio \(16:7\) pins down only the sizes relative to each other, so write the counts as \(16k\) prints and \(7k\) paintings for one unknown multiplier \(k\).
Apply both changes first, then set the new ratio equal to \(5:3\). Cross-multiplying gives \(3(16k-26)=5(7k+13)\).
review.sol: With \(16k\) prints and \(7k\) paintings, the new ratio gives \(3(16k-26)=5(7k+13)\), so \(48k-78=35k+65\), then \(13k=143\) and \(k=11\). The gallery held \(176\) prints and \(77\) paintings, and afterwards \(150\) and \(90\), a total of \(\boxed{240}\). The check is that \(150:90\) reduces to \(5:3\), and the total fell from \(253\) because 26 works left and only 13 came in.

review.x: A cabinet holds oak, ash and birch dowels and nothing else, with oak to ash \(9:5\) and ash to birch \(15:8\). After 105 more birch dowels arrive, the birch count equals the ash count. Enter the total number of dowels the cabinet held before that delivery.
hints: Combine the two ratios into one three-part ratio first, since the ash is written as \(5\) in one statement and \(15\) in the other.
The chain is \(27:15:8\). Writing the counts as \(27k\), \(15k\) and \(8k\), equal counts after the delivery give \(8k+105=15k\).
review.sol: Triple \(9:5\) to get \(27:15\), so both statements now use \(15\) for the ash and oak to ash to birch is \(27:15:8\). With the counts \(27k\), \(15k\) and \(8k\), equal counts after the delivery mean \(8k+105=15k\), so \(7k=105\) and \(k=15\). The parts total \(50\), so the cabinet held \(50(15)=\boxed{750}\). The counts are \(405\) oak, \(225\) ash and \(120\) birch, and \(120+105=225\) as required.

blocks.x: A conversion factor is a ratio of one amount to itself written in two units, so it is worth \(1\). One gallon and four quarts are the same volume, so \(\frac{4\text{ qt}}{1\text{ gal}}\) has equal volumes above and below the bar. Multiplying by it is multiplying by \(1\), which changes the unit and not the amount. The first two problems give the fraction.

A fuel tank holds 46 gallons, and \(1\text{ gal}=4\text{ qt}\). Multiply \(46\text{ gal}\) by \(\frac{4\text{ qt}}{1\text{ gal}}\), writing the unit inside the fraction so that gal above the bar cancels against gal below it. Enter the tank's capacity in quarts.
hints: Write \(46\text{ gal}\) as \(\frac{46\text{ gal}}{1}\), so gal sits above the bar in the amount and below the bar in the factor.
Once gal cancels, what is left is \(46\times 4\) with qt as the only unit remaining.
blocks.sol: Cancelling gal above against gal below leaves \(46\times 4\) quarts, so the capacity is \(\boxed{184}\). A quart is smaller than a gallon, so more of them cover the same volume, and \(184\) is larger than \(46\) as it has to be.

blocks.x: A second tank on the same lot holds 268 quarts. The same fact \(1\text{ gal}=4\text{ qt}\) also gives the factor \(\frac{1\text{ gal}}{4\text{ qt}}\), which has qt below the bar. Multiply by that factor and enter this tank's capacity in gallons.
hints: Write the tank as \(\frac{268\text{ qt}}{1}\), so qt is above the bar. It cancels only against a factor with qt below the bar.
After qt cancels, the arithmetic left is \(268\div 4\) and gal is the only unit remaining.
blocks.sol: Cancelling qt above against qt below leaves \(268\div 4\) gallons, so the capacity is \(\boxed{67}\). The two factors are one fact written two ways, and which one to use depends on which unit has to cancel.

blocks.x: A conversion factor is worth \(1\). Divide both sides of \(1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}\) by \(1\text{ ft}\) and the left side becomes \(1\), so \(1=\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}\). Divide the same equality by \(12\text{ in}\) instead and \(1=\frac{1\text{ ft}}{12\text{ in}}\). So every stated equality between two units gives two fractions, each worth \(1\), and each the other turned upside down. Multiplying an amount by either one multiplies it by \(1\), which leaves the amount alone and changes only the unit it is written in.

A pallet of bolts weighs 592 ounces, and \(1\text{ lb}=16\text{ oz}\). The two factors available are \(\frac{16\text{ oz}}{1\text{ lb}}\) and \(\frac{1\text{ lb}}{16\text{ oz}}\), and only one of them cancels the ounces. Enter the weight in pounds.
hints: Write the weight as \(\frac{592\text{ oz}}{1}\), so oz is above the bar. Only a factor with oz below the bar cancels it.
A pound is heavier than an ounce, so the number of pounds is smaller than \(592\). Multiplying by \(16\) cannot be right.
blocks.sol: The factor with oz below the bar is \(\frac{1\text{ lb}}{16\text{ oz}}\), and cancelling oz leaves \(592\div 16\), so the weight in pounds is \(\boxed{37}\). The other choice gives \(9472\) and leaves the label \(\frac{\text{oz}^2}{\text{lb}}\), which is not a weight.

blocks.x: A recording runs 1020 seconds, and \(1\text{ min}=60\text{ s}\). A student multiplies \(1020\text{ s}\) by \(\frac{60\text{ s}}{1\text{ min}}\) and reports that the recording is 61200 minutes long. Enter the correct length in minutes.
hints: Check the units in the student's product. Multiplying \(1020\text{ s}\) by a factor with s on top gives s times s, so nothing cancels and the label left over is \(\frac{\text{s}^2}{\text{min}}\).
The s in \(1020\text{ s}\) cancels only against an s on the bottom. The fact \(1\text{ min}=60\text{ s}\) also gives the factor \(\frac{1\text{ min}}{60\text{ s}}\), which has s there.
blocks.sol: Multiplying by \(\frac{1\text{ min}}{60\text{ s}}\) cancels s and leaves \(1020\div 60\), so the length in minutes is \(\boxed{17}\). The student used the reciprocal factor, so the result is \(3600\) times too large, and the leftover label \(\frac{\text{s}^2}{\text{min}}\) is not a time.

blocks.x: Units cancel like common factors. Write the unit symbol inside the fraction and treat it as one more factor in the product. A unit above the bar and the same unit below divide out exactly as the \(7\) does in \(\frac{5\times 7}{3\times 7}\), and the units that remain are the units of the result. The choice between the two forms is then settled by which unit has to cancel, not by remembering whether to multiply or divide. Put the unwanted unit below the bar and the wanted unit above it.

blocks.cap: The word days appears once in the amount and once below the fraction bar, so it divides out the way a shared number does, and \(42\div 7=6\) is what the arithmetic leaves. The length of time did not change, only the unit it is written in.

blocks.x: Not every pair of units has a fact stated directly between them. Sometimes one fact runs from the starting unit to a middle unit, and a second fact runs from that middle unit to the one wanted. The next two problems take that route, the first through one middle unit and the second through two.

A gym orders 8 coils of climbing rope, with \(1\text{ coil}=30\text{ m}\) and \(1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}\). Neither fact is a direct coil-to-centimeter conversion. Multiply the 8 coils by two conversion factors in a row and enter the total length in centimeters.
hints: The unit meters is common to both given facts, so the chain is coils to meters to centimeters, one factor for each step.
The chain is \(8\text{ coils}\times\frac{30\text{ m}}{1\text{ coil}}\times\frac{100\text{ cm}}{1\text{ m}}\), with coil below the bar in the first factor and m below the bar in the second.
blocks.sol: Cancelling coils gives \(8\times 30=240\) meters, and cancelling meters gives \(240\times 100\), so the length in centimeters is \(\boxed{24000}\). Both factors equal \(1\), so the two together equal \(1\) as well, and the rope has the same length as before, only measured in a smaller unit.

blocks.x: A recipe is written in cups and the jug in the kitchen is marked in milliliters. Use \(1\text{ cup}=16\text{ tablespoons}\), \(1\text{ tablespoon}=3\text{ teaspoons}\) and \(1\text{ teaspoon}=5\text{ mL}\). Enter the volume of 6 cups in milliliters.
accept: one thousand four hundred and forty
hints: Three stated facts give three factors, run in the order cups to tablespoons to teaspoons to milliliters, and each factor carries the unit you already have below the bar so that unit cancels.
Tablespoons and teaspoons are both intermediate units and both cancel, and what is left is \(6\times 16\times 3\times 5\).
blocks.sol: Cancelling cups, then tablespoons, then teaspoons leaves \(6\times 16\times 3\times 5\), so the volume in milliliters is \(\boxed{1440}\). Multiplying the three factors together first gives \(16\times 3\times 5=240\), so the whole chain is the single factor \(\frac{240\text{ mL}}{1\text{ cup}}\), and any number of cups then takes one step.

blocks.x: Chains of conversion factors. Multiplying by several factors in a row converts an amount through intermediate units. Write each factor so the unit just produced is below the bar, and stop when only the wanted unit remains. Each factor is worth \(1\), so their product is worth \(1\) and the amount is unchanged however many factors it takes. Counts named by ordinary nouns cancel the same way, since \(1\text{ coil}=30\text{ m}\) is an equality between two descriptions of one length just as \(1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}\) is.

A rate is written with one unit above the bar and a different one below, so it carries two units at once. The next problems change both of them. Speeds, flow rates and rates of pay all have this shape, and a pace written as time over distance is the same information as a speed written as distance over time.

A conveyor belt runs at 48 meters per minute. Use \(1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}\) and \(1\text{ min}=60\text{ s}\). Both units change, so two factors are needed. Enter the speed in centimeters per second.
hints: Write the speed as \(\frac{48\text{ m}}{1\text{ min}}\). The m to be removed sits above the bar and the min to be removed sits below it, so the two factors go in the opposite way up from each other.
The chain is \(\frac{48\text{ m}}{1\text{ min}}\times\frac{100\text{ cm}}{1\text{ m}}\times\frac{1\text{ min}}{60\text{ s}}\).
blocks.sol: Cancelling m above against m below and min below against min above leaves \(\frac{48\times 100}{60}\), so the speed in centimeters per second is \(\boxed{80}\). The minutes factor goes in as \(\frac{1\text{ min}}{60\text{ s}}\) and not the other way up, since the min to be removed starts below the bar and cancels against a copy above it.

blocks.x: In 1793 France fixed the meter as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the pole along the meridian through Paris. Delambre and Mechain spent seven years surveying that arc to set the length.
A runner's watch reports a pace of 3 minutes 45 seconds per kilometer, which is \(\frac{225\text{ s}}{1\text{ km}}\). Use \(1\text{ h}=3600\text{ s}\). Enter the speed in kilometers per hour.
hints: The unit asked for has km above the bar and h below it, so the pace's s has to cancel and an h has to arrive, and the one fact available for both is \(1\text{ h}=3600\text{ s}\).
Turned over the pace is \(\frac{1\text{ km}}{225\text{ s}}\), and multiplying that by \(\frac{3600\text{ s}}{1\text{ h}}\) cancels s and leaves km above the bar with h below it.
blocks.sol: Turning the pace over gives \(\frac{1\text{ km}}{225\text{ s}}\), and multiplying by \(\frac{3600\text{ s}}{1\text{ h}}\) cancels s and leaves \(3600\div 225\), so the speed in kilometers per hour is \(\boxed{16}\). Turning a rate over states the same information with the two quantities exchanged, and \(16\times 225=3600\) checks it, since sixteen kilometers at \(225\) seconds each take exactly one hour.

blocks.x: Converting a rate changes two units at once. A rate is a fraction with unlike units above and below the bar, so multiplying by one factor changes one of them and leaves the other. Two are needed. The top unit cancels against a copy of itself below the bar of one factor, and the bottom unit against a copy above the bar of the other, so the two factors are written the opposite way up. Turning a rate over exchanges the two quantities without changing the information, so a pace in time per distance and a speed in distance per time are one fact written two ways.

An area is a length times a length, so converting an area means converting both lengths, and the same factor is used twice. Write \(1\text{ yd}^2\) as \(1\text{ yd}\times 1\text{ yd}\) and replace each yard on its own. A volume is three lengths multiplied, so the same factor is used three times.

A patio covers 34 square yards, and \(1\text{ yd}=3\text{ ft}\). One square yard is \(1\text{ yd}\times 1\text{ yd}\), so convert each of the two lengths and see how many square feet one square yard holds. Enter the patio's area in square feet.
hints: A square yard is a square measuring 3 ft along each side, so count the square feet inside one of them first.
One square yard is \(3\times 3=9\) square feet, so the factor is \(\frac{9\text{ ft}^2}{1\text{ yd}^2}\).
blocks.sol: One square yard is \(3\text{ ft}\times 3\text{ ft}=9\text{ ft}^2\), so the factor is \(\frac{9\text{ ft}^2}{1\text{ yd}^2}\) and the area is \(34\times 9=\boxed{306}\). Using the length factor once gives \(102\) and leaves the label \(\text{yd}\cdot\text{ft}\), since only one of the two lengths was converted.

blocks.x: A shipping crate has a volume of 5 cubic feet, and \(1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}\). Enter the crate's volume in cubic inches.
hints: One cubic foot is a cube whose edges each measure \(12\) inches, so converting the edge length alone is not enough.
One cubic foot is \(12\times 12\times 12=1728\) cubic inches.
blocks.sol: One cubic foot is a cube with \(12\)-inch edges, so it is \(12\times 12\times 12=1728\) cubic inches, and the volume is \(5\times 1728=\boxed{8640}\). Using the conversion factor of \(12\) once gives \(60\) and twice gives \(720\), but a volume is three lengths multiplied together, so the factor belongs in the product three times.

blocks.x: Squared and cubed units. A square unit is one length multiplied by a length equal to it. Replace each of those two lengths by the \(k\) smaller units it equals and the product becomes \(k\times k\) of the smaller square unit, so the numeric factor is used once per length and ends up squared. A cubic unit is a product of three lengths, so the same replacement leaves \(k\times k\times k\). Written as factors, an area is multiplied by the conversion factor twice and a volume three times, which is why an area conversion is never just \(k\).

A conversion factor can be built from any stated equality between two amounts, and the two amounts need not be the same kind of thing. A price, a rate of pay, and a count per container are all equalities of that kind, so each one has two factors, and the choice between them comes down to the unit that has to cancel.

A field technician is paid 35 dollars per hour and works 6 hours per shift. Each of those statements gives a conversion factor, one between hours and dollars and one between shifts and hours. Enter the pay in dollars for 8 shifts.
accept: one thousand six hundred and eighty
hints: Start from 8 shifts and pick the factor that cancels shifts, which leaves hours.
The chain is \(8\text{ shifts}\times\frac{6\text{ hours}}{1\text{ shift}}\times\frac{35\text{ dollars}}{1\text{ hour}}\).
blocks.sol: Cancelling shifts and then hours leaves \(8\times 6\times 35\), so the pay in dollars is \(\boxed{1680}\). Shifts and hours are both units of time, while dollars and hours are not, and nothing about the method changes, since 35 dollars per hour states that one hour of work goes with 35 dollars the way one foot goes with 12 inches.

blocks.x: A trading post prices goods in four measures, with \(1\text{ varn}=7\text{ sedge}\), \(1\text{ sedge}=3\text{ pell}\) and \(5\text{ pell}=2\text{ quill}\). The last fact has no \(1\) on either side. A merchant holds 15 varn. Enter the value in quill.
hints: Three facts and three factors. Take varn to sedge, sedge to pell, then pell to quill, each one written with the unit you are getting rid of below the bar.
\(15\times 7=105\) sedge, then \(105\times 3=315\) pell. Only one orientation of the last factor cancels pell, so use that one.
blocks.sol: Chaining \(15\text{ varn}\times\frac{7\text{ sedge}}{1\text{ varn}}\times\frac{3\text{ pell}}{1\text{ sedge}}\times\frac{2\text{ quill}}{5\text{ pell}}\) cancels varn, sedge and pell in turn and leaves \(\frac{15\times 7\times 3\times 2}{5}\), so the value in quill is \(\boxed{126}\). Using the last factor upside down gives \(315\times\frac{5}{2}=787.5\), with pell uncancelled and no quill in the answer.

blocks.x: Every conversion here was a multiplication by a fraction worth \(1\), chosen so the unwanted unit appeared above the bar and below it, and in the area and volume cases the same factor was used twice or three times. Lesson 6.3, Percents, uses a ratio whose second part is always \(100\). The question there is what an amount is being compared against.

review.x: A sack of rice has a mass of 9000 grams, and \(1\text{ kg}=1000\text{ g}\). Enter the mass in kilograms.
hints: Both \(\frac{1000\text{ g}}{1\text{ kg}}\) and \(\frac{1\text{ kg}}{1000\text{ g}}\) equal \(1\), so multiplying by either one is legal. Only one of the two cancels the grams.
For the grams to cancel, for the grams to cancel, grams has to be in the denominator of the fraction, and the unit left over is then kilograms.
review.sol: Multiplying by \(\frac{1\text{ kg}}{1000\text{ g}}\) cancels the grams and gives \(\frac{9000}{1000}\), so the mass in kilograms is \(\boxed{9}\). The other fraction, \(\frac{1000\text{ g}}{1\text{ kg}}\), also equals \(1\), but it gives \(9000000\) with units of \(\frac{\text{g}^2}{\text{kg}}\), which is not a mass.

review.x: A spool carries 4500 centimeters of thread, and \(1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}\). Enter the length of the thread in meters.
hints: Write the amount as \(\frac{4500\text{ cm}}{1}\). The cm to be removed sits above the bar there, so the factor has to carry cm below the bar.
The factor with cm below the bar is \(\frac{1\text{ m}}{100\text{ cm}}\), and multiplying by it cancels cm and leaves a division by \(100\).
review.sol: Cancelling cm leaves \(4500\div 100\), so the length in meters is \(\boxed{45}\). A meter is longer than a centimeter, so the count of meters is the smaller number.

review.x: A bench is 156 inches long, and \(1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}\). Multiplying by \(\frac{12\text{ in}}{1\text{ ft}}\) gives \(1872\), a number far larger than the length in inches, and leaves the label \(\frac{\text{in}^2}{\text{ft}}\). Pick the factor that cancels inches instead and enter the length in feet.
hints: Inches appear above the bar twice in the student's product, once in the length and once in the factor, so there is nothing to cancel and the label left over is \(\frac{\text{in}^2}{\text{ft}}\).
The factor needed here is \(\frac{1\text{ ft}}{12\text{ in}}\), with inches below the bar to cancel the inches in \(156\text{ in}\). The arithmetic is then \(156\div 12\).
review.sol: Multiplying by \(\frac{1\text{ ft}}{12\text{ in}}\) cancels the inches and leaves \(156\div 12\), so the length in feet is \(\boxed{13}\). The student's factor has inches above the bar as well, so nothing cancels and the label on \(1872\) is \(\frac{\text{in}^2}{\text{ft}}\), not feet.

review.x: A bakery counts its rolls in dozens and has 51 dozen, with \(1\text{ dozen}=12\text{ rolls}\). Multiply by a conversion factor that cancels dozen, and enter the number of rolls.
hints: The starting quantity carries the unit dozen, so dozen goes in the denominator of the conversion factor and rolls in the numerator.
The factor is \(\frac{12\text{ rolls}}{1\text{ dozen}}\), so the product reads \(51\text{ dozen}\times\frac{12\text{ rolls}}{1\text{ dozen}}\).
review.sol: The factor \(\frac{12\text{ rolls}}{1\text{ dozen}}\) cancels dozen, so the number of rolls is \(51\times 12=\boxed{612}\). The flipped factor \(\frac{1\text{ dozen}}{12\text{ rolls}}\) would leave \(51\div 12\), which is why dozen belongs in the denominator.

review.x: A stationery order is 12 boxes, where \(1\text{ box}=20\text{ packs}\) and \(1\text{ pack}=50\text{ envelopes}\). Enter the number of envelopes in the order.
hints: The order runs boxes to packs to envelopes, so two conversion factors apply one after the other.
\(12\times 20=240\) packs, and each pack holds \(50\) envelopes.
review.sol: Writing \(12\text{ boxes}\times\frac{20\text{ packs}}{1\text{ box}}\times\frac{50\text{ envelopes}}{1\text{ pack}}\) and cancelling boxes and then packs leaves \(12\times 20\times 50\), so the number of envelopes is \(\boxed{12000}\). Each box holds \(20\times 50=1000\) envelopes, so the order is \(12\times 1000\), a quick check on the size.

review.x: A warehouse holds 8400 bottles, packed at \(1\text{ case}=12\text{ bottles}\) and \(1\text{ pallet}=25\text{ cases}\). Enter the number of full pallets.
hints: Write the first factor with bottles in the denominator and cases on top, so the bottle unit divides out of \(8400\).
\(8400\div 12=700\) cases. One more factor turns cases into pallets.
review.sol: Cancelling bottles and then cases leaves \(\frac{8400}{12\times 25}=\frac{8400}{300}\), so the number of full pallets is \(\boxed{28}\). Both factors go in with the old unit underneath, \(\frac{1\text{ case}}{12\text{ bottles}}\) and then \(\frac{1\text{ pallet}}{25\text{ cases}}\), which is the same order the two facts are written in.

review.x: A delivery is 9 crates, with \(1\text{ crate}=6\text{ trays}\), \(1\text{ tray}=8\text{ punnets}\) and \(1\text{ punnet}=15\text{ berries}\). Enter the number of berries.
accept: six thousand four hundred and eighty
hints: Three factors, crates to trays to punnets to berries. In each one the unit being removed is below the bar and the new unit above it.
\(9\times 6=54\) trays and \(54\times 8=432\) punnets.
review.sol: Cancelling crates, trays and punnets in turn leaves \(9\times 6\times 8\times 15\), so the number of berries is \(\boxed{6480}\). Each of the three factors is worth \(1\), so the delivery is the same size either way and only the thing being counted is different.

review.x: A tap fills a tank at 12 liters per minute, and \(1\text{ h}=60\text{ min}\). Enter the fill rate in liters per hour.
hints: The liters are the same in both rates, and only the time unit changes, so one conversion factor is enough.
In 12 liters per minute the min is on the bottom, so pick a factor with min on top, and that factor is \(\frac{60\text{ min}}{1\text{ h}}\).
review.sol: Multiplying by \(\frac{60\text{ min}}{1\text{ h}}\) cancels the min and gives \(12\times 60\), so the rate in liters per hour is \(\boxed{720}\). Dividing by \(60\) instead gives \(0.2\), which is the wrong direction, since more liters come out in an hour than in a minute.

review.x: A snail moves 3 centimeters per second. Use \(1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}\) and \(1\text{ h}=3600\text{ s}\). Enter the speed in meters per hour.
hints: Both units have to change, so the chain needs two factors, one turning centimeters into meters and one turning seconds into hours.
In one hour the snail covers \(3\times 3600=10800\) centimeters, and every meter is \(100\) centimeters.
review.sol: \(\frac{3\text{ cm}}{1\text{ s}}\times\frac{1\text{ m}}{100\text{ cm}}\times\frac{3600\text{ s}}{1\text{ h}}\) cancels cm and s and leaves \(\frac{3\times 3600}{100}\), so the speed in meters per hour is \(\boxed{108}\). Each conversion factor is a fraction equal to \(1\), so multiplying by it changes the units and not the speed.

review.x: A conveyor carries 900 kilograms per hour. Use \(1\text{ kg}=1000\text{ g}\) and \(1\text{ h}=60\text{ min}\). Enter the rate in grams per minute.
hints: Write the rate as \(\frac{900\text{ kg}}{1\text{ h}}\). Each conversion factor is a fraction equal to \(1\), so pick the orientation that clears kg from above the bar and h from below.
\(900\times 1000=900000\) grams in an hour, spread over \(60\) minutes.
review.sol: Cancelling kg and h leaves \(\frac{900\times 1000}{60}\), so the rate in grams per minute is \(\boxed{15000}\). The hours factor goes in as \(\frac{1\text{ h}}{60\text{ min}}\) rather than \(\frac{60\text{ min}}{1\text{ h}}\), since the h below the bar cancels only against an h above it.

review.x: A courtyard covers 7 square meters, and \(1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}\). Enter the area in square centimeters.
hints: A square meter is a square 100 cm along each side, so the length factor is used twice.
One square meter is \(100\times 100=10000\) square centimeters.
review.sol: One square meter is \(100\text{ cm}\times 100\text{ cm}=10000\text{ cm}^2\), so the area is \(7\times 10000=\boxed{70000}\). Converting only one of the two lengths gives \(700\), which is too small by a factor of \(100\).

review.x: A poster covers 4320 square inches. Use \(1\text{ ft}=12\text{ in}\). Enter the area in square feet.
hints: One square foot is a square 12 in along each side.
\(12\times 12=144\), so divide by \(144\) and not by \(12\).
review.sol: One square foot is \(144\text{ in}^2\), so the area is \(4320\div 144=\boxed{30}\). Dividing by \(12\) once gives \(360\), which is not an area in square feet.

review.x: A planter holds 2 cubic yards of soil, and \(1\text{ yd}=3\text{ ft}\). Enter the volume of that soil in cubic feet.
hints: A cubic yard is the volume of a cube \(3\text{ ft}\) along each edge.
\(3\times 3\times 3=27\), so one cubic yard is \(27\) cubic feet.
review.sol: One cubic yard is \(3\text{ ft}\times 3\text{ ft}\times 3\text{ ft}=27\text{ ft}^3\), so the volume is \(2\times 27=\boxed{54}\). The factor between cubic yards and cubic feet is \(3^3=27\), not \(3\), since a volume is a product of three lengths.

review.x: Paint costs 38 dollars per can, and one can covers 25 square meters of wall. A job needs 300 square meters of wall painted. Enter the cost of the paint for that job, in dollars.
hints: Two factors are needed, square meters to cans and then cans to dollars. In each one, put the unit you want to cancel below the bar.
The first factor is \(\frac{1\text{ can}}{25\text{ m}^2}\), and it gives \(300\div 25=12\) cans.
review.sol: Cancelling square meters and then cans in \(300\text{ m}^2\times\frac{1\text{ can}}{25\text{ m}^2}\times\frac{38\text{ dollars}}{1\text{ can}}\) leaves \(12\times 38\), so the cost in dollars is \(\boxed{456}\). The unit cans sits above the bar in one factor and below it in the next, so it divides out and dollars is the only unit left.

review.x: A carpenter is paid 26 dollars per hour and works 4 hours per session, and has earned 1560 dollars from those sessions alone. Enter the number of sessions worked.
hints: Dollars have to cancel, so the pay rate goes in with dollars below the bar.
\(1560\div 26=60\) hours, and each session is \(4\) hours.
review.sol: \(1560\text{ dollars}\times\frac{1\text{ h}}{26\text{ dollars}}\times\frac{1\text{ session}}{4\text{ h}}\) cancels dollars and hours and leaves \(\frac{1560}{26\times 4}\), so the number of sessions is \(\boxed{15}\). Both stated rates go in upside down from how they are written, because the chain runs from dollars back to sessions.

review.x: Each team at a school has 6 students, each bus carries 4 teams, and the school fills 9 buses for a meet. Enter the number of students the school sends.
hints: Each rate can be written as a fraction, and buses, teams and students cancel exactly as units of measure do.
Start from \(9\text{ buses}\) and chain both rates, \(9\text{ buses}\times\frac{4\text{ teams}}{1\text{ bus}}\times\frac{6\text{ students}}{1\text{ team}}\).
review.sol: Chaining the two rates gives \(9\text{ buses}\times\frac{4\text{ teams}}{1\text{ bus}}\times\frac{6\text{ students}}{1\text{ team}}\), and buses and teams cancel to leave \(9\times 4\times 6=\boxed{216}\). Per bus that is \(4\times 6=24\) students, and \(9\times 24=216\).

review.x: On a game map, \(1\text{ span}=9\text{ notches}\), \(4\text{ notches}=3\text{ pips}\) and \(1\text{ pip}=20\text{ steps}\). A road is 8 spans long. Enter its length in steps.
hints: Three conversion factors run spans to notches to pips to steps, and the middle fact has a number on both sides rather than a \(1\).
Eight spans is \(8\times 9=72\) notches, and the middle factor multiplies by \(3\) and divides by \(4\).
review.sol: Chaining the three factors leaves \(\frac{8\times 9\times 3\times 20}{4}\), so the length in steps is \(\boxed{1080}\). The middle factor is \(\frac{3\text{ pips}}{4\text{ notches}}\), with notches in the denominator to cancel the \(72\) notches from the first step. The flipped factor \(\frac{4\text{ notches}}{3\text{ pips}}\) gives \(1920\) instead.

blocks.x: What an amount is compared against is called the base, the number a percent is taken of. Twelve percent of one base and twelve percent of another are different amounts, so a percent alone leaves the amount unknown. Prealgebra chapter 9 did the arithmetic. New here is naming an unknown with a letter, which turns a percent sentence into an equation.
A quality check clears \(64\%\) of a shipment. Percent means per hundred, so \(64\%\) is the ratio \(\frac{64}{100}\). Reduce it to lowest terms and enter the fraction.
hints: Both parts of a ratio can be divided by the same number without changing it, and \(64\) and \(100\) share a factor larger than \(2\).
That factor is \(4\), so divide above and below the bar by \(4\), then check whether the result reduces again.
blocks.sol: Dividing both parts by \(4\) gives \(\frac{64}{100}=\boxed{\frac{16}{25}}\). Since \(16\) and \(25\) share no common factor above \(1\), that is lowest terms. As a decimal it is \(64\div 100=0.64\), the same number with the point moved two places left.

blocks.x: A sensor logs \(\frac{7}{20}\) of its readings as out of range. A percent is a ratio whose second part is \(100\), so rewrite \(\frac{7}{20}\) with \(100\) below the bar. Enter the percent, just the number.
hints: Multiplying both parts of a ratio by the same number leaves it unchanged, so find the factor that turns the \(20\) below the bar into \(100\).
\(20\times 5=100\), so multiply above the bar by \(5\) as well.
blocks.sol: Multiplying both parts by \(5\) gives \(\frac{7}{20}=\frac{35}{100}\), so the percent is \(\boxed{35}\). A second route gives the same number, \(\frac{7}{20}\times 100=35\), and it still works when the denominator does not divide \(100\).

blocks.x: A percent is a ratio whose second part is \(100\). The symbol \(\%\) means per hundred, so \(p\%\) is the ratio \(p:100\), the number \(\frac{p}{100}\). Everything 6.1 established about ratios holds here unchanged, so multiplying both parts by the same number leaves the value alone, and \(\frac{7}{20}\) and \(\frac{35}{100}\) are one number written twice. With the second part fixed at \(100\) for every percent, comparing two percents is comparing their first parts and nothing else.

A label states that a bottle of saline is \(6.5\%\) salt by mass, so the ratio of salt to total mass is \(\frac{6.5}{100}\). Lowest terms means the top and the bottom are whole numbers with no common factor other than \(1\). Enter \(6.5\%\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Multiplying the top and the bottom by the same number does not change the value, and multiplying by \(10\) removes the decimal point.
That gives \(\frac{65}{1000}\), and \(65\) and \(1000\) share a factor of \(5\).
blocks.sol: Multiplying the top and the bottom by \(10\) gives \(\frac{6.5}{100}=\frac{65}{1000}\), and dividing both by \(5\) gives \(\boxed{\frac{13}{200}}\). Since \(13\) is prime and does not divide \(200\), that is lowest terms. As a decimal it is \(0.065\).

blocks.x: A machinist finds that \(\frac{5}{6}\) of a batch passes inspection. That fraction is already in lowest terms and no whole number times \(6\) gives \(100\), so it cannot be rescaled to a whole number over \(100\). Multiply \(\frac{5}{6}\) by \(100\) anyway and enter the exact percent as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Rescaling is blocked here, so the route left is plain arithmetic. Multiplying \(\frac{5}{6}\) by \(100\) multiplies the numerator by \(100\) and leaves the \(6\) underneath alone.
\(\frac{5}{6}\times 100=\frac{500}{6}\), and \(500\) and \(6\) are both even.
blocks.sol: \(\frac{5}{6}\times 100=\frac{500}{6}\), and dividing the numerator and the denominator by \(2\) gives \(\boxed{\frac{250}{3}}\). The same percent is often written \(83\frac{1}{3}\%\). Long division gives \(250\div 3=83.333\ldots\), which never terminates, so \(83.3\%\) and \(83.33\%\) are roundings while \(\frac{250}{3}\%\) is exact.

blocks.x: Percent, fraction and decimal. Percent to fraction, write \(\frac{p}{100}\), clear any decimal above the bar by multiplying both parts by \(10\), then reduce. Percent to decimal, divide by \(100\), which moves the point two places left. Fraction or decimal to percent, multiply by \(100\), since \(x=\frac{100x}{100}\) and the first part of that ratio is the percent. When a fraction in lowest terms has a denominator with a prime factor other than \(2\) or \(5\), its decimal repeats, so the exact percent is a fraction such as \(\frac{250}{3}\) and every decimal form of it is a rounding.
